newsitem.title: USA: Clinton convenes emergency Mideast peace summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton convenes emergency Mideast peace summit.

text.p: Leaders of Israel, the Palestinians and Jordan converged on the White House for a crisis summit on Tuesday as President Bill Clinton struggled to prevent a collapse of the Middle East peace process.

Clinton, who interrupted his high-flying re-election campaign to lead the emergency diplomatic effort, scheduled separate 30-minute meetings with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the Oval Office to start the summit.

Arafat arrived in Washington about 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT) after stops in Egypt and Luxemburg for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak -- who declined to attend the summit -- and European ministers on last week's eruption of Arab-Israeli violence in the West Bank and Gaza and the fraying of Israel-Palestinian peace accords.

Arafat was meeting privately in Washingtn with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa before the White House meetings. Moussa was representing Mubarak in Washington during the summit although he was not taking a direct opart in the talks.

Before leaving Luxemburg, Arafat told reporters he would attend the Washington summit with "no conditions or ultimatums." But there were unconfirmed reports in Israel that he had sent a letter to Clinton listing five demands.
The separate summit meetings were to be followed by a group encounter involving Clinton, Arafat Netanyahu and King Hussein of Jordan, who met one-on-one with the president on Monday night.
Follow-on talks were to occur later on Tuesday and Wednesday at the White House and Blair House, a government guest house for distinguished foreign visitors just across Pennsylvania Avenue.
U.S. officials said all sides agreed to hold public statements to a minimum to try to encourage progress.
Some delegation representatives said they had been asked to say nothing to the press until the summit's conclusion.

U.S. officials played down chances for a dramatic breakthrough in the talks, which grew out of last week's violence in the West Bank, Gaza and Jerusalem. Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israelis were reported killed in five days of clashes after Israel opened a pedestrian tunnel to archaeological sites near Jerusalem's Temple Mount, sacred to both Judaism and Islam.

"It's clear to me that the Middle East peace process is in a state of crisis," said Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has devoted much of his energies to trying to end the region's ancient strife.
Christopher said the goal of the summit was to convince the parties "to talk together again" and "find the basis for resuming negotiations" on stalled peace efforts.
Clinton's room for manoeuvre was limited by the pressures of the November 5 U.S. election campaign, which pits him against Republican Bob Dole.

While Dole took a seemingly supportive stance, he also warned against any arm-twisting of the Jewish state. "Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order," he said in a statement.
Meantime, Dole campaign aides made it clear that they were ready to accuse Clinton of a major foreign policy fumble if the summit failed.

One of the highlights of Clinton's presidency was his shepherding of Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin into a "historic handshake" at 1993 White House ceremonies in which Israel and the Palestinians signed a peace accord designed to end a long and bloody feud.
Clinton, however, favoured former Prime Minister Shimon Peres in Israel's May elections, leaving him with limited influence in his dealings with Netanyahu.

Ironically, the summit opened almost a year to the day after another Washington summit on the Middle East at which Rabin sealed a deal with Arafat that set out specific steps to implement the framework peace agreement signed in 1993.

One month later Rabin was assassinated. Then in February and March of this year, Islamic suicide bombers killed 59 people in attacks against Israel, paving the way for the election of a more hardline Israeli government under Netanyahu. The peace process has been stalled since then.
